notes: Ruling slot 13 = PPM (sole legal party since 1965). Kadihines in 19 (Maoist-leaning). Ba'athists in 21 following MD's placement of the Ba'athist National Vanguard Party. Nasserists in 7, Nahda veterans in 6. Armed forces use MD sprite.

0.name: La Coopération
0.text:
La Coopération is the web of French technical advisers, seconded magistrates, military instructors and Paris-trained Mauritanian officials that has framed the state since independence in 1960. Under the cooperation accords, French officers still help run the army, French teachers staff the lycées, and the currency sits inside the CFA franc zone managed from Paris.

Its members favour keeping Mauritania anchored in the franc zone, protecting French as the language of administration and resisting the pressure of radical students and Arab nationalists to revise the accords. Its leverage lies in budget subsidies, in the Central Bank of West African States and in the iron-ore revenues of MIFERMA, which depend on European buyers.

1.name: La Vieille Garde
1.text:
La Vieille Garde gathers the notables of the former Mauritanian Progressive Union (UPM), the conservative, French-backed party that dominated the territory in the 1950s before it was absorbed into the ruling party. Sidi el-Moktar N'Diaye, the colony's first deputy in the French National Assembly, remains its best-known figure, though its members now sit quietly inside the PPM.

They favour close ties with France and the West, a cautious pace of Arabization, respect for tribal and maraboutic hierarchies and an economy built on livestock and iron ore. Their weight rests on clan networks in the Trarza and Brakna and on their standing with French advisers and the older generation of administrators.

2.name: Le Manifeste des 19
2.text:
Le Manifeste des 19 takes its name from the declaration signed in early 1966 by nineteen Black Mauritanian officials protesting against compulsory Arabic in secondary schools and against what they saw as Moorish domination of the state. The text followed strikes by Black pupils and deadly clashes in Nouakchott, and its signatories were sanctioned by the regime.

Its milieu is the francophone, largely Halpulaar, Soninke and Wolof civil service of the Senegal River valley. It calls for equal treatment of the national communities, bilingual education with French kept as a working language, protection of civil liberties and an open, Western-leaning foreign policy. Its leverage lies in the administration, the schools and kinship ties across the river into Senegal.

3.name: Les Instituteurs du Fleuve
3.text:
Les Instituteurs du Fleuve are the francophone primary and secondary teachers of the Senegal River valley and of Kaédi, Rosso and Nouakchott, the best organized educated workforce in the country. Their strikes against the 1966 language reform made them one of the few civilian groups to defy the single party openly, and their union militants remain under close watch.

They argue for social democracy on the French model: free and bilingual public schooling, collective bargaining, fair wage scales for civil servants and an elected assembly with real powers. Abroad they favour ties with Senegal and the francophone West. Their influence comes from the classroom, from teacher training colleges and from links to Senegalese unions.

4.name: Fédération des étudiants d'Afrique noire en France
4.english: Federation of Black African Students in France
4.native_full: Fédération des étudiants d'Afrique noire en France
4.text:
The Federation of Black African Students in France, founded in 1950, is the radical, anti-colonial association of African students in Paris, Toulouse and other French cities. Its Mauritanian members, a few hundred young men on state scholarships, return each summer with pamphlets, Soviet-bloc literature and contempt for the single party, and some have studied in Moscow and Eastern Europe.

The Mauritanian section demands nationalization of the MIFERMA iron mines, withdrawal from the franc zone, revision of the cooperation accords with France and alignment with the socialist camp. Its leverage is small but concentrated: the future engineers, teachers and officials without whom the state cannot be governed.
4.wiki: Federation of Black African Students in France

5.name: Les Mineurs de Zouérate
5.text:
Les Mineurs de Zouérate are the iron-ore workers of the MIFERMA mines at Kédia d'Idjil, the largest wage-earning workforce in Mauritania. In May 1968 a strike over pay and living conditions ended when the army opened fire on the miners, killing several, and the shooting turned the mining town into a symbol for the country's young radicals.

Militants among the miners and the railwaymen of the Zouérate–Nouadhibou line demand nationalization of the mines, equal pay with European staff, independent unions and an end to the ruling party's control over labour. They have no legal organization, but they can stop the ore trains that carry most of the country's export earnings.

6.name: Les Anciens de la Nahda
6.text:
Les Anciens de la Nahda are former members of the Mauritanian National Renaissance Party, founded in 1958 as an Arab nationalist, anti-French party that looked to Morocco and the Arab East. The party was suppressed and its leaders jailed before it was absorbed into the ruling party in 1961; its best-known figure, Ahmed Baba Miské, has since served the regime as a diplomat.

Its veterans want Mauritania defined as an Arab state, Arabic as the sole official language, an end to French military and cultural tutelage and solidarity with the Arab world against Israel and the West. Their influence rests on Moorish students, Arabic teachers and merchants with ties to Cairo and Rabat.

7.name: Al-Nasiriyyun
7.text:
Al-Nasiriyyun are the young Arab nationalists of Nouakchott and Atar who take Gamal Abdel Nasser as their model. Educated in Cairo, Damascus and Baghdad or in Arabic-language schools at home, they organize in clandestine cells among students, junior officers and teachers, outside the ruling party's control.

They seek a strong, centralized Arab republic led by a disciplined vanguard, rapid Arabization of schools and administration, nationalization of foreign mining concessions and close alignment with Egypt and the anti-imperialist camp, including arms and credits from the Soviet Union. Their leverage lies in the army's junior ranks, the Arabic teaching corps and the prestige of Cairo among the Moorish population.

8.name: Les Libanais de Nouakchott
8.text:
Les Libanais de Nouakchott are the small community of Lebanese Shia traders who run import houses, hardware stores and transport firms in Nouakchott, Nouadhibou and Rosso, most of them with family roots in South Lebanon and kin across Senegal. They have no political organization, but their elders follow closely the rise of Imam Musa al-Sadr, who in 1969 became head of the new Supreme Islamic Shia Council in Beirut.

They favour a reformed, socially engaged Shi'ism, protection of minority traders, good relations with the state and quiet neutrality between East and West. Their leverage is commercial: credit, imports and the remittance networks linking West Africa to Beirut.

9.name: Cercle de Najaf
9.text:
Le Cercle de Najaf is a handful of young Lebanese Shia in Nouakchott and Nouadhibou who correspond with relatives studying at the seminaries of Najaf, where the exiled Iranian cleric Ruhollah Khomeini has taught since 1965. They meet in private homes to read religious tracts and reject the commercial quietism of their elders.

The circle holds that clerics must guide political life, condemns the Shah and Western influence in the Muslim world, and admires the hard line of the Najaf seminaries against secular regimes. It numbers a few dozen at most and has no structure, but it can draw on remittance money and on the prestige of clerics visiting West Africa.

10.name: al-Tariqa al-Qadiriyya
10.text:
The Qadiriyya is the oldest Sufi brotherhood in Mauritania, organized around maraboutic lineages such as the Ahl Cheikh Sidiya of Boutilimit, the Trarza town that is also President Ould Daddah's birthplace. Alongside its rival the Tijaniyya, it dominates the mahadras, the desert schools of Islamic law and Arabic letters, and provides much of the clergy of the Islamic Republic.

Its sheikhs back the regime in exchange for respect for Islamic law in personal status matters, support for Arabic education and the authority of religious families over their followers. They distrust both secular leftists and imported Islamist doctrines. Their leverage lies in the loyalty of tens of thousands of disciples and the mediation they offer between tribes and the state.

11.name: Al-Murabitun
11.text:
Al-Murabitun is a loose network of itinerant preachers and mahadra students who invoke the Almoravids, the eleventh-century movement of Saharan warrior-ascetics that rose in what is now Mauritania and conquered Morocco and Muslim Spain. Without a leader of national standing, it circulates sermons condemning the secular state, French advisers and the bars of Nouakchott.

Its members call for a single Islamic polity uniting the western Sahara and the Maghreb under sharia and reject both the Western and Soviet blocs as godless. They regard the borders drawn by France as illegitimate. Their reach is limited to remote camps and oases, but they draw on a deep popular memory of holy war against Christian rule.

12.name: Les Azharis
12.text:
Les Azharis are the young Mauritanians returning from Al-Azhar in Cairo and from universities in Saudi Arabia, Kuwait and Damascus with diplomas and contacts in the Muslim Brotherhood. They teach Arabic and religion in Nouakchott's secondary schools, gather in study circles in private homes and keep apart from the single party.

They want an Islamic society built from the base: modern religious education, moral reform, zakat as social welfare and a state that applies sharia through elected institutions. They oppose both French secular influence and Marxist students, and look to the Gulf for funding. Their leverage lies in schools and mosques and in growing Saudi interest in the Sahel.

13.name: Parti du Peuple Mauritanien
13.text:
The Mauritanian People's Party was formed in December 1961 from the merger of the Mauritanian Regroupment Party, the Nahda and smaller groups, and became the sole legal party in 1965. Its founder and secretary-general, President Moktar Ould Daddah, governs through its political bureau, while the National Assembly is elected on a single list.

The party preaches national unity between Moors and Black Africans, cautious Arabization, Islam as state religion and non-alignment, keeping French aid while opening to China, the Arab world and the Eastern bloc. It draws strength from tribal notables, civil servants and the president's personal authority, and is absorbing unions, women's and youth organizations into its structures.

14.name: Les Notables du Fleuve
14.text:
Les Notables du Fleuve are the chiefs, landholding lineages and religious families of the Halpulaar, Soninke and Wolof villages along the Senegal River, from Rosso to Sélibaby. They rallied to the ruling party in the early 1960s in return for local authority, but remain wary of Moorish dominance in Nouakchott after the language crisis of 1966.

They defend customary land tenure in the flood-recession farmlands, the authority of village chiefs and imams, and the place of their communities in the state. Indifferent to the Cold War blocs, they look across the river to Senegal for trade and family ties. Their leverage is control of the country's only farming belt and of rural mobilization.

15.name: Société des Mines de Fer de Mauritanie
15.native_full: Société des Mines de Fer de Mauritanie
15.text:
MIFERMA is the consortium of French, British, Italian and West German steel and mining interests that has exploited the iron-ore deposits of Kédia d'Idjil since 1963, shipping the ore by a 650-kilometre railway to the port of Nouadhibou. It is by far the largest enterprise in Mauritania and provides the bulk of its exports and a large share of state revenue.

Its management favours stable government, the franc zone, low taxation of exports and firm handling of strikes, as shown at Zouérate in 1968. It cooperates with the regime but fears calls for nationalization. Its leverage lies in revenue, foreign exchange and the European steel markets on which the country depends.

16.name: Les Négociants de Nouakchott
16.text:
Les Négociants de Nouakchott are the Moorish trading families who have moved from the caravan towns of the Adrar and Tagant into the new capital and Nouadhibou, dealing in cloth, tea, sugar, livestock and imported goods. Linked by tribe and religious brotherhood, they finance commerce across the Sahara and into Senegal, Mali and the Canary Islands.

They want low tariffs, freedom of trade, few state monopolies, access to bank credit for Mauritanian rather than French firms and a light hand from customs officials. They keep away from the Cold War and prefer pragmatic deals with the government. Their leverage is the cash economy of the capital and the credit that sustains nomadic herders.

17.name: Les Pasteurs du Sahel
17.text:
Les Pasteurs du Sahel are the nomadic and semi-nomadic camel and cattle herders of the Hodh, Assaba and Tagant, still the majority of Mauritanians. Since 1968 failing rains have dried up wells and pastures, pushing families toward the river valley and the shantytowns of Nouakchott, and elders blame overgrazing around new boreholes and towns.

They call for protection of pastures and wells, controls on charcoal burning and tree felling, fair access to water points and state help to keep herds alive through drought. They are wary of both blocs and of the mining economy, which offers them little. Their influence lies in their numbers and in tribal councils the ruling party must consult.

18.name: Union des Travailleurs de Mauritanie
18.text:
The Union of Mauritanian Workers is the country's main trade-union federation, formed in 1961 from earlier unions affiliated to French and African centres. It organizes dockers, civil servants, teachers and the miners and railwaymen of MIFERMA, but since the Zouérate shootings of 1968 it has been pressed to subordinate itself to the ruling party.

Its leaders argue for an African socialism compatible with Islam: higher wages, Mauritanization of skilled jobs, social security and a larger state share in mining profits. They favour non-alignment and good relations with Algeria and the Arab world. The federation's strength lies in its ability to halt the mines, the port and the administration, which a radical rank and file urges it to use.

19.name: Al-Kadihin
19.text:
The Kadihines, the 'toilers', are the clandestine Marxist movement taking shape among students, young teachers and workers since the student strikes and the Zouérate shootings of 1968. Unlike older nationalist groups, it recruits across the Moorish and Black communities and circulates mimeographed tracts in Arabic and French in Nouakchott, Nouadhibou and the mining towns.

Inspired by Mao Zedong and the Chinese revolution, it denounces the single party as a neo-colonial regime and demands nationalization of MIFERMA, exit from the franc zone, revision of the French accords and a national democratic revolution led by workers and peasants. Its leverage lies in schools, lycées and the mining unions, where it is quickly displacing the old leadership.

20.name: Les Arabisants
20.text:
Les Arabisants are the Arabic-educated teachers, clerks and party officials who led the campaign that made Arabic compulsory in secondary schools in 1966. Many come from Moorish maraboutic families and mahadra schooling and resent the French-speaking elite, Moorish and Black alike, that still holds the senior posts in the administration.

They demand full Arabization of education, courts and administration, preference for Arabic speakers in recruitment and a public culture rooted in Islam and the Moorish heritage. They distrust France, the francophone south and Marxist students alike. Their leverage lies in the ruling party's lower ranks, the radio and the Arabic press, and in popular resentment of French cultural dominance.

21.name: Al-Ba'thiyyun
21.text:
Al-Ba'thiyyun are small clandestine cells of Mauritanian students and teachers recruited by the Arab Socialist Ba'ath Party during their studies in Damascus and Baghdad. They operate in secrecy inside Arabic-language schools and among junior civil servants, and look to the Iraqi Ba'ath, in power since July 1968, for scholarships and guidance.

They preach a single Arab nation from the Atlantic to the Gulf with Mauritania as its western frontier, a disciplined vanguard party above tribe and region, and an authoritarian socialist state. They are hostile to France, Israel and the United States, and suspicious of the Black southern elite. Their leverage is ideological intensity and Iraqi money rather than numbers.

22.name: Armée nationale mauritanienne
22.text:
The Mauritanian Armed Forces are a small army of a few thousand men, formed in 1960 and still trained and partly officered by French cooperants. They garrison the northern desert along the Spanish Sahara, guard the iron-ore railway and were used to break the Zouérate miners' strike in 1968. The officer corps is young, largely Moorish and loyal to President Ould Daddah.

The officers favour order, national unity and modernization under firm leadership, and resent meagre budgets and dependence on France. They are anti-communist but not bound to either bloc. Their leverage is that they are the only national institution with arms, transport and radio across the whole territory.

23.name: Les Émirats maures
23.text:
The Moorish Emirates of Trarza, Brakna, Adrar and Tagant are the warrior dynasties that ruled the western Sahara before the French conquest and kept their titles under colonial rule. The Republic has stripped the emirs of formal power, but they remain heads of great Hassaniya-speaking confederations and command deference from warrior and tributary lineages.

They want recognition of traditional authority, respect for the hierarchy of warrior, marabout and tributary groups and consultation on land, pasture and justice. They accept the Republic as long as it leaves them their prestige, and look to the Moroccan throne as the model of a Muslim monarchy. Their leverage lies in tribal loyalty and the support they bring the ruling party.
